blocks.text: There follows a chapter whose title in Latin is De haren carmen, but in Arabic في حيوانان بحريان [fī ḥayawānān baḥriyyān], On sea serpents. And what is meant is σμύραινα [smyraina], muraenae [morays], which the same author calls سوريا [sūriyā]. But the Latin translator here has semurion, and thinks that a doctor was so named, although σμύραινα [smyraina] is a fish. That my conjecture is correct will be plain to those who compare Aëtius with Avicenna. For there Avicenna reproduces the very words of Aëtius about the moray fish.

[III, 225] The title of the following chapter is De Alhatraf et Hauden, which again they hold to be among the kinds of dragons. But in the Arabic there is طروغورون [ṭrūghūrūn] truguron, for which read طروغون [ṭrūghūn], τρύγων [trygōn], that is, the sea stingray; that this is the subject is apparent from a comparison of the same Aëtius with Avicenna. So much for the benefit of the lovers of Arabic. Now from the digression back to the road.
